5. The respondent Nos. 1, 2 and 5 in contesting this matter have primarily focused on the issue that the respondent No. 2 is a subsequent bona fide purchaser of the above-referred 990 shares for good consideration and without any notice of the Agreement or any interest arising under the same. Proceeding on the premise that the petitioner did indeed sell the 990 shares to the respondent No. 3 for a consideration of Taka 99,000 by executing a Form-117 on 30-6-1991 (Annexure-'X-1) and that this transfer was approved by the BoD on 1-7-1991 (as brought on record under Anne-xure-'X-2'), the respondents in their Affidavit-in-Opposition assert that the minutes of the BoD meeting dated 1-7-1991 though bearing a specific reference to "threadbare discussions" having taken place regarding, inter alia, the transfer of the petitioner's shares to the respondent No. 3, however, bear no mention of either the petitioner or the respondent No. 3 having ever placed the BoD and the Company on notice either of the existence of the Agreement that, according to the petitioner, constitutes the basis of such transfer of shares to the respondent No. 3 or indeed, of the fact of a part of the consideration money for such transfer constituting a repayment of a loan obtained by the Company from the petitioner, thereby, potentially affecting the Company's interest. The respondents contend that such lack of candor on the part of both the petitioner and the respondent No. 3 at the BoD meeting of 1-7-1991, and as evident upon a clear reading of the minutes/resolution of the BoD meeting of that date (Annexure-'X-2'), as to the existence of the Agreement and the ostensible indebtedness of the Company to the petitioner, is merely representative of the fact that the transfer of shares was effected between the petitioner and the respondent No. 3 without reference to any agreement whatsoever. In this regard, the respondents contend that even if it were to be accepted that said transfer took place in accordance with the terms of any alleged agreement. It may be deduced that the petitioner and the respondent No. 3 had therefore, deliberately not been forthcoming about the existence of the Agreement from the very beginning and chose to reveal the existence of the same at a moment more opportune for themselves given that the respondent No. 2 and the Company were put on notice of the same much later and for the first time by the petitioner's letter dated 16-8-1999 addressed to the respondent No. 2 Managing Director with an attested copy of the Form-117 executed by the Court on 18-5-1999 with a view to registering his 990 shares (Annexure-'F'). 

 6. The dispute in this case arises with the subsequent transfer, with Other Suit No. 42 of 1994 being pendent at the time, by the respondent No. 3 of 1180 shares, including the disputed 990 shares, to the respondent No. 2 by executing a Form 117 on 15-3-1995 (Annexure-'X3') and as approved by a BoD resolution of the same date (Annexure-'X-5'). From the minutes of the said BoD meeting it is also evident that the respondent No. 3 also, inter alia, transferred 700 shares to the respondent No. 4 Nazir Ahmed thereby leading to the respondent No. 4 becoming a shareholder director in the Company (Annexure-'X-5'). It is shown by reference to the minutes of the Bode meeting dated 24-6-1997 that the respondent Nos. 3 and 4 were among four shareholders who transferred their shares to the respondent No. 2 leading to the approval of the resignation of the respondent Nos. 3 and 4 as Managing Director and Director respectively (Annexure-'X-6'). Such a transfer of his shares by the respondent No. 3 constituting a transfer of his entire shareholding in the Company, led to the respondent No. 3 effectively resigning from the Company (Annexure-1X-8'). The spate of transfers of shares and consequential resignations led to the Company having two shareholders being the respondent No. 2 and his wife the respondent No. 5 who assumed the responsibilities of Managing Director and Chairman respectively with effect from 24-6-1997 as evident, for example, from the relevant Form-XII Particulars of the Directors etc. (Annexure-'X-7'). The petitioner having claimed in his Affidavit-in-Reply that these transfers, in fact, constitute secret, sham or antedated transfers, the respondents have generally submitted on the authenticity of all these transaction given that the requisite and necessary documents in evidence of such transactions have been duly submitted with the respondent No. 6, the Registrar, Joint Stock Companies and Firms and as is submit-ted to be evident further from endorsements to that effect by the Office of the Registrar on the said filed documents. It is also generally sub-mitted by the respondents that such filings, as evidenced variously in Annexures 'X-1' to 'X-9', having been duly submitted to the Registrar long before the ex parte decree was passed on 26-5-1998 in Other Suit No. 42 of 1994, the petitioner had ample opportunity to know about the transactions recorded therein as should have prompted the petitioner at least to inform the Company at the earliest possible opportunity about the Agreement, the pendency of the Suit and/or the consequential decree, instead of waiting until 16-8-1999 after the execution of the Form 117 through the Court on 18-5-1999. It is also respondents case that the filings above brought these documents into the domain of public inspection by reason of which the petitioner ought to have had ample notice of the said documents and should have consequentially taken reasonable steps to implead the Company and/or the respondent No. 2 in the Sun or to have, at the very least, issued notices upon them once the last date for payment by the respondent No. 3 under the Agreement had expired. This the petitioner appears not to have done and these lapses on the part of the petitioner so to do have led the respondents to conclude that the petitioner got the Form-117 executed by the Court surreptitiously on 18-5-1999. It is on this general ground that the respondents pray for this application to be rejected. 

 8. The starting point for a consideration of this case must be one where the petitioner armed with a decree of the lower Court executed in the form of a Form-117, finds himself pitted against the respondent No. 2 who asserts to be the bona fide purchaser or transferee of the same said 990 shares without notice of the Agreement. In this regard, this Court has at the behest of the learned Advocates for the petitioner and the respondents. Mr Kamal-ul-Alam and Mr Sheikh Hasan Arif respectively, extensively considered all documents with a view to ascertaining the justifiability of claims by either side as to the lack of authenticity of records and documents relied upon by the other. Consequent upon a lengthy and painstaking process, including an examination of the Order Sheets in their entirety of Other Suit No. 42 of 1994 obtained from the Court of the Joint District Judge. First Court, Sadar, Chittagong , this Court is generally satisfied as to the authenticity of all documents produced and relied upon by the parties. In this regard, it merits mention that an earlier attempt by this Court to secure a transmission of the entire file/records of Other Execution Case No. 6 of 1998 arising out of Other Suit No. 42 of 1994 proved futile given that the Joint District Judge. First Court, Sadar, Chittagong by a letter dated 4-10-2007 informed this Court of all such records having been destroyed by the time this Court passed its Order on 30-9-2007. 

 "It is a discretion of the Court to see whether the point at issue relating to rectification of share register can be resolved on the basis of materials on record. If the case is complicated and very doubtful and if it appears that without resorting to some procedure other than the summary proceeding under section 38 of the Act a case cannot be disposed of, the Company Court should not interfere with such a matter. But if it is apparent on the face of the record that legal rights of the parties are clear and can be settled on the basis of the materials on record, the Company Court can exercise its jurisdiction in the matter." 

 Notwithstanding the wide-ranging facts and questions as to the authenticity of documents raised in this case, thus Court is of the opinion that this matter essentially is one, and as succinctly submitted by the learned Advocate for the respondents Mr Sheikh Hasan Arif, of this Court having to deal with two competing transferees of the same set of shares and vying with each other for this Court's attention. Further, Mr Arif's submissions as to upholding the sanctity of information discernible both from the Company's own records and those filed with the Registrar have struck a favourable chord with this Court. In this regard, given the facts and circumstances of this case, it has not been lost on this Court, and as argued by Mr Arif that delayed information and notice received both by the Company and the respondent No. 2 of the fact of the Agreement, the subsequent Suit and decree and the Court-executed Form 117 have struck the Company like a bolt from the blue, thereby, exposing the vulnerability and susceptibility of a company as this as well as of its members to that which Mr Arif submits are unseemly attacks perpetrated by the petitioner. In that regard, this Court is of the view that it is indeed, well within the authority and jurisdiction of this Court to decide on this Application under section 43 of the Act. 

 10. Admittedly, the petitioner having only decided upon putting the Company and the respondent No. 2 on notice of the Court's decree in Other Suit No. 42 of 1994 and of the Court-executed Form-117 at a very late stage, that of itself begs the question as to why the petitioner had not been equally forthcoming at the due and proper time with information on the Agreement pertaining to matters of transfer of shares, loan to the Company, refund, reversion of shares, etc. at least on 1-7-1991 when the Boded to decide on the issue of the transfer of 990 shares and approved the same after a threadbare discussion. No satisfactory explanation has been forthcoming from the petitioner in this regard to dispel the notion possibly of a fraud sought to be perpetrated on the Company both by the petitioner and the respondent No. 3 in collusion with each other. Against this backdrop, it has not been difficult for this Court to salvage from the facts of this case the issues of competing rights of the parties as are clearly discernible from the documents made available and, thereby, to consider the primacy of one set of rights relative to the other. 

 12. With the above obstacle out of the way, it has not been difficult for this Court to appreciate in the facts and circumstances that the right of the petitioner under the Agreement, if it is true and valid, though earlier in time, is only an equitable right and does not affect the rights and interests of a subsequent transferee as the respondent No. 2, should the respondent No. 2 be considered a bona fide purchaser or transferee for valuable consideration without notice of that equitable right. The test of such bona fide acquisition has been enunciated in a long line of precedents, among which this Court has taken particular note of the judgment and ratio in Abdul Khaleque vs Md Fazlul Huq reported in 26 DLR 247. This Court notes, in particular, that the facts in the Abdul Khaleque Case follow a pattern and dynamics similar to the one at hand.
